definition.text: Push technology, or server push, is a way of communicating in which the server, rather than the client, starts the exchange.

facts.text: In push the server initiates communication, which differs from the pull method where the client initiates it.

Clients usually state which information they want through the publish-subscribe model: a client subscribes to channels on a server, and the server pushes new content to subscribed clients automatically.
When restrictive security policies block incoming HTTP requests, push is sometimes simulated by polling, in which the client periodically checks the server for new information.
Instant messaging and synchronous conferencing are push services: chat messages are pushed to the user as soon as the messaging service receives them.
Email is partly push: SMTP is a push protocol, but the last step from mail server to desktop usually uses a pull protocol such as POP3 or IMAP, which clients poll frequently.
IMAP's IDLE command lets the server tell the client when new messages arrive.
Push-enabled web applications include software updates, stock tickers, webchat, auctions, online betting and gaming, sport results, monitoring consoles and sensor network monitoring.

definition.text: To get real-time updates from an HTTP server, either the browser does the work by polling, or the browser and server cooperate over WebSocket or server-sent events.

facts.text: An HTTP server cannot automatically initiate a connection to a browser, so the browser is the initiator.
Web applications were built around a client-server model in which the client always starts a transaction, so the server had no way to push data without first receiving a request.
One family has the browser do the heavy lifting with short polling or long polling; the other has server and browser cooperate through WebSocket or server-sent events.
With short polling the browser keeps retrying until it gets the latest data; with long polling the server does not return a result until new data has arrived.
With WebSocket or SSE, the server can send the latest data straight to the browser once the connection is established.
SSE is uni-directional, so the browser cannot send a new request to the server, while WebSocket is full-duplex, so the browser can keep sending new requests.

title: Long polling

definition.text: In long polling the client sends a request and the server holds it open until new information is available or a timeout is reached, then responds so the client can immediately ask again.

facts.text: If the server has nothing new when the poll arrives, it holds the request open instead of sending an empty response, and replies only when information is available or a timeout threshold is reached.

Once it has new information the server sends an HTTP response that completes the open request, and the client immediately (or after a defined interval) issues another request to re-establish a pending connection.
Long polling is not true push: it emulates server push where real push is not possible, such as sites whose security policies reject incoming HTTP requests.
Unlike normal polling, it removes the response latency between information becoming available and the client's next request.
It is easy to implement, nearly universally supported and good for small-scale projects, but usually not scalable: every response needs a new connection, which is intensive on the server.
Reliable message ordering can be an issue across multiple requests, and latency grows because the server must wait for a new request before it can send again.

notes: Wikipedia says long polling eliminates polling's response latency; Singh lists increased latency as a disadvantage. Different baselines (plain polling vs a held connection), so not a conflict.

sources.title: Long polling, WebSockets, Server-Sent Events (SSE) (Singh's System Design)

definition.text: Polling means repeatedly checking an external device or service for its status, as a synchronous activity driven by the client, to retrieve updated information.

facts.text: Polling is like constantly asking whether there is anything new, even when there may be no update, so it is resource-intensive and inefficient.
The client gets updates only when it asks, so it can miss real-time information, but developers have more control over when and how data is fetched.
With short polling the browser keeps retrying until it gets the latest data; polling is a solid option when an infrastructure limitation prevents the use of webhooks.

Busy-wait polling does nothing except check status until the device is ready; checking repeatedly and returning to another task wastes fewer cycles but is generally less efficient than interrupt-driven I/O.
The polling cycle is the time in which each element is monitored once; the best cycle depends on the desired speed of response and on the overhead of polling, such as processor time and bandwidth.
Polling fails to scale when there are too many devices to check: the time needed to poll them can exceed the time available to service them.
Roll call polling queries each element in a fixed sequence and needs a timeout so silent elements cannot lock it up; it is inefficient when overhead is high and few of many elements are active.

The alternative is interrupts, signals from devices that say they need attention; in many situations, such as multitasking operating systems, interrupts are more efficient because they cut processor spinning and bandwidth use.

definition.text: A webhook is an endpoint in your application server that you hand to an external service as a callback, so the service calls it whenever something interesting happens.

facts.text: Instead of continuously asking for information, you create an endpoint in your application server and give it as a callback to the external service, such as a payment processor or a shipping vendor.
Every time something interesting happens, the external service calls the endpoint and provides the information.
Data is pushed to the application as soon as it is available, which makes webhooks ideal for real-time updates.
Webhooks are recommended for applications that need instant data delivery and are efficient in resource use, especially in high-throughput environments.
Network issues can cause missed notifications, so webhooks need proper retry mechanisms.
Webhooks are triggered by events such as a code push, a purchase or a blog comment, and because they use HTTP they fit into web services without new infrastructure.

The receiver should authenticate each incoming POST against spoofing and check its timestamp against replay, using an HMAC signature in a header, a shared secret, mutual TLS, basic authentication, or a sender IP list that is not sufficient alone.

Because a sender lets users set an arbitrary destination URL, OWASP names webhooks a common vector for server-side request forgery; the mitigation is to re-check the resolved IP before each delivery, not only at registration.

definition.text: Server-sent events (SSE) is a server push technology in which a client receives automatic updates over an HTTP connection and the server can start sending data once the connection is established.

facts.text: The client requests a URL through the JavaScript EventSource API to receive an event stream, whose media type is text/event-stream; the API is standardized in the HTML Living Standard by the WHATWG.
The client makes a request, the connection stays open, and the server sends events whenever new data is available.
SSE is unidirectional: once the client has sent its request it can only receive responses, not send new requests over the same connection.
It is simple to implement for both client and server, supported by most browsers, and causes no trouble with firewalls.
Limits: the unidirectional nature, a cap on the number of open connections, and no support for binary data.
When sending high-frequency data the server must manage backpressure to avoid saturating clients, using client-side buffering, adaptive rate limiting that adjusts event frequency, or event batching.
Designs for real-time messaging and live location tracking can use either WebSockets or SSE.

definition.text: HTTP server push, also called HTTP streaming, is a way of sending unsolicited asynchronous data from a web server to a web browser.

facts.text: The server does not close the connection after serving the response, so an event can go out immediately; otherwise it would be queued until the client's next request.
It can be built on chunked transfer encoding, or on the multipart/x-mixed-replace MIME type, which browsers treat as a document that changes whenever the server pushes a new version.
In the pushlet technique the server never ends the response and periodically sends snippets of JavaScript that update the page, so the client needs no Java applet or plug-in.
A drawback of pushlets is that the server cannot control browser timeouts, and a timeout forces a page refresh.

definition.text: A push notification is a message pushed from a back-end server or application to a user interface such as a mobile or desktop application.

facts.text: Push notifications are either local, where the application schedules the notification with the device's OS, or remote, where a server sends them.

For a remote notification the client application registers on the server with a unique key, such as a UUID or Apple Device Token, and the server sends the message against that key over a protocol such as HTTP or XMPP.
On arrival a notification can show a short message, set a badge on the app icon, light the notification LED or play an alert sound.
Typical content is chat messages, vendor special offers, event reminders and changes to subscribed topics such as the weather.
Real-time push notifications may raise privacy issues, since they can be used to link social network pseudonyms to the real identities of smartphone owners.

definition.text: A notification system takes notifications from business services, validates and schedules them, and delivers them through channels such as in-app messages, email, SMS and social media pushes.

facts.text: It covers in-app notifications, email notifications, SMS and OTP notifications, and social media pushes.
Business services send notifications to a notification gateway, which can take one notification at a time or batches of them.

The gateway forwards notifications to a distribution service that validates, formats and schedules them according to settings; a template repository pre-defines message formats and a channel preference repository pre-defines preferred delivery channels.
Notifications then go to routers, normally message queues, and channel services pass them to the internal and external delivery channels.
A tracking and analytics service captures delivery metrics so the operations team can view reports and improve the user experience.

definition.text: Web push is the set of web standards that deliver real-time events such as incoming calls or messages to a user, based on a simple protocol over HTTP/2.

facts.text: Radio use is a major drain on mobile devices, and separate persistent connections with their keep-alive traffic waste it, so Web push consolidates all events into one session through a single service that distributes them as they arrive.

The model has three actors: a user agent, a push service and an application server; the user agent creates a subscription and gives it to its application server, and it is the basis of all later interactions.

A subscription is two resources: a private subscription resource the user agent uses to receive messages and delete the subscription, and a public push resource shared with the application server to send messages.

The user agent POSTs to the push service to subscribe and gets 201 Created; the application server POSTs the message body to the push resource; the user agent GETs its subscription and the service answers with HTTP/2 server push.

For at-least-once delivery the user agent MUST acknowledge each message with an HTTP DELETE; an application server can ask for delivery confirmation with Prefer: respond-async, which the push service MUST support.

Web Notifications, a W3C standard, alert the user outside a web page, and the W3C Push API gives web applications the push service; Chrome, Firefox and Edge implement it fully, Safari partly (February 2023).

definition.text: WebSocket is a communications protocol that gives a bidirectional channel over a single TCP connection.

facts.text: The channel is a persistent connection that stays open, so client and server can each send data at any time, independently of the other.
It gives full-duplex interaction with lower overhead than half-duplex alternatives such as HTTP polling, because the server can send content without being asked first.

Before WebSocket, two-way web apps polled over several HTTP connections and sent upstream messages as separate calls, which meant multiple TCP connections per client, an HTTP header on every message and client-side tracking of replies.

RFC 6455 describes an independent TCP-based protocol: a thin layer adding an origin-based security model, naming, framing and a closing handshake; HTTP servers only see its handshake, as an Upgrade request.
TCP alone deals with streams of bytes with no inherent notion of a message; WebSocket enables streams of messages on top of TCP.
It suits games, stock tickers, multiuser applications with simultaneous editing, and user interfaces that expose server-side services in real time.
Advantages: full-duplex asynchronous messaging, a better origin-based security model, and light weight for both client and server.
Terminated connections are not automatically recovered, and older browsers lack support, though modern major browsers support the standardized protocol.

title: WebSocket opening handshake

definition.text: The WebSocket opening handshake is an HTTP Upgrade request from the client and a 101 response from the server, after which the connection switches to the WebSocket protocol.

facts.text: The client's handshake is an HTTP GET Upgrade request (HTTP version at least 1.1), so one port can serve both HTTP clients and WebSocket clients.
The request carries Host, Upgrade: websocket, Connection: Upgrade, a Sec-WebSocket-Key of 16 random bytes base64-encoded, Sec-WebSocket-Version 13, and an Origin header from browser clients.
The server must prove it received the handshake, so that it does not accept connections that are not WebSocket connections, such as crafted XMLHttpRequest or form submissions.
To prove it, the server appends a fixed GUID to the Sec-WebSocket-Key value, takes the SHA-1 hash, base64-encodes it and returns it in Sec-WebSocket-Accept.

The server replies 101 (Switching Protocols); any other status means the handshake has not completed and HTTP semantics still apply, and the client sends no frames if the Sec-WebSocket-Accept value is missing or wrong.

A server that rejects the handshake MUST return an HTTP error: for example 403 Forbidden for an unwanted origin, 426 Upgrade Required with its supported versions for a wrong version, or 404 Not Found for an unavailable service.
After the 101 response HTTP stops being used and communication switches to a binary frame-based protocol, in which both sides can send data in either direction.

A WebSocket can also be established over HTTP/2 with the extended CONNECT method of RFC 8441, which carries it in one stream so other streams keep carrying HTTP traffic; RFC 9220 adapts this for HTTP/3.

conflicts.text: Sec-WebSocket-Key and Sec-WebSocket-Accept are intended to prevent a caching proxy from re-sending a previous WebSocket conversation, and provide no authentication, privacy or integrity.
conflicts.note: Wikipedia gives a different purpose; the fact above follows RFC 6455, which says the server proves it read the handshake.

notes: Wikipedia and RFC 6455 differ on why the key/accept exchange exists; the RFC's version is stated and Wikipedia's is in conflicts.

sources.title: Long polling, WebSockets, Server-Sent Events (SSE) (Singh's System Design)

definition.text: After the opening handshake WebSocket exchanges messages made of one or more frames, which are either data frames (text or binary) or control frames (Close, Ping, Pong).

facts.text: Once the handshake is done, either side may send data messages (text or binary) and control messages (Close, Ping, Pong) at any time.

The protocol is frame-based rather than stream-based, with minimal framing; a message is one frame if unfragmented or two or more if fragmented, and intermediaries may split or coalesce frames, so endpoints must not depend on frame boundaries.
Fragmentation lets a sender start a message of unknown length without buffering it; without it the whole message must be buffered so its length can be counted before the first byte is sent.

An unfragmented message is one frame with FIN set and a non-zero opcode; a fragmented one starts with FIN clear and a non-zero opcode, continues with opcode 0 frames, and ends with an opcode 0 frame that has FIN set.

Fragments must arrive in order and must not interleave with another message's fragments unless an extension allows it; control frames may be injected between fragments, so a ping is not stuck behind a large message, but are never fragmented.
A frame header has a FIN bit, three reserved bits that must be 0 unless an extension defines them, a 4-bit opcode, a mask bit, a payload length, and a 32-bit masking key when the mask bit is 1.
Payload length uses 7 bits for 0 to 125; the value 126 means the next 16 bits hold the length and 127 means the next 64 bits do.
Opcodes are 0 continuation, 1 text, 2 binary, 8 Close, 9 Ping and 10 Pong; the protocol defines six frame types and reserves ten.

title: WebSocket masking
article: rfc>6455#10. Security Considerations > 10.3. Attacks On Infrastructure (Masking)

definition.text: WebSocket masking is the rule that a client XORs every frame it sends to the server with a random 32-bit key, so a script cannot control how its data looks on the wire.

facts.text: A client MUST mask all frames it sends to the server, whether or not TLS is used; a server MUST NOT mask the frames it sends, and a server MUST close the connection on receiving an unmasked frame.
Masking XORs each payload byte with the key byte at index i modulo 4 of a 32-bit masking key chosen by the client; the same algorithm masks and unmasks.
The client MUST choose a fresh masking key for every frame from a strong entropy source; unpredictability stops authors of malicious applications from selecting the bytes that appear on the wire.

The reason is an experiment in which attackers poisoned caching proxies by sending data on an upgraded connection that looked like an HTTP GET; masking client data stops a script making a message that an intermediary misreads as HTTP.

title: WebSocket ping and pong
article: rfc>6455#5. Data Framing > 5.5. Control Frames > 5.5.2. Ping

definition.text: Ping and Pong are WebSocket control frames used as keepalive and heartbeat, to check that the other endpoint is still responsive.

facts.text: Either side may send a Ping at any time after the connection is established and before it is closed; it can serve as a keepalive, a latency measurement or a check that the remote endpoint is responsive.
An endpoint that receives a Ping MUST answer with a Pong, unless it already received a Close frame, as soon as practical, and the Pong must carry the same application data as the Ping.
A Pong may also be sent unsolicited as a unidirectional heartbeat, and no response to it is expected; a Pong with no prior Ping is ignored.

definition.text: The WebSocket closing handshake is an exchange of Close frames in which either peer asks to close and the other answers before the TCP connection is shut.

facts.text: Either peer can start by sending a Close control frame (opcode 8); the other replies with a Close frame if it has not already sent one, and both peers may safely start it at the same time.
After sending a Close frame a peer sends no more data frames; after receiving one it discards further data.
Once an endpoint has both sent and received Close it MUST close the TCP connection: the server immediately, the client ideally after waiting for the server to do so.
It complements the TCP closing handshake, which is not always reliable end-to-end with intercepting proxies, and avoids cases where data is lost unnecessarily.
Servers MAY close the connection whenever they want, but clients SHOULD NOT close it arbitrarily; either way closure begins with the closing handshake.
A Close frame may carry a 2-byte status code followed by a UTF-8 reason of at most 123 bytes; clients MUST NOT show the reason to end users.

Defined codes include 1000 normal closure, 1001 going away, 1002 protocol error, 1003 unsupported data, 1007 invalid payload data, 1008 policy violated, 1009 message too big and 1011 internal server error.

Codes 1005, 1006 and 1015 are reserved and MUST NOT be sent in a Close frame; 1000 to 2999 belong to the protocol, 3000 to 3999 to libraries and frameworks registered with IANA, and 4000 to 4999 to private use.

title: WebSocket security

definition.text: WebSocket security rests on the browser's Origin header, TLS (wss) and server-chosen client authentication, because WebSocket requests are not covered by the same-origin policy.

facts.text: Unlike regular cross-domain HTTP requests, WebSocket requests are not restricted by the same-origin policy.

The Origin header tells the server which script origin made the request; a server meant only for certain sites SHOULD verify the origin is one it expects, and SHOULD answer an unacceptable origin with HTTP 403 Forbidden.
Without an origin check, cross-site WebSocket hijacking, similar to cross-site request forgery, is possible when the connection is authenticated with cookies or HTTP authentication.

The origin check ensures trusted browsers running malicious JavaScript cannot fake a handshake; it does not stop non-browser clients, which can send any Origin, so a server must not trust that any input is valid.
The protocol prescribes no client authentication: a server can use cookies, HTTP authentication or TLS authentication, and tokens are better when sensitive data is sent.
Confidentiality and integrity come from running over TLS (wss URIs); implementations MUST support TLS and SHOULD use it.
Incoming data MUST always be validated by both clients and servers; text messages must be valid UTF-8, and an endpoint that finds invalid UTF-8 MUST fail the connection.

A malicious endpoint can try to exhaust memory or mount denial of service with one huge frame or a long stream of small fragments, so implementations MUST protect themselves against exceeding their limits and SHOULD cap frame and message sizes.

conflicts.text: WebSocket servers must validate the Origin header against the expected origins during connection establishment.
conflicts.note: Wikipedia says must; RFC 6455 says a server that is not meant to process input from any web page SHOULD verify the Origin.

notes: Origin validation: Wikipedia says 'must', RFC 6455 section 10.2 says SHOULD; the RFC wins.

definition.text: WebSocket is unaware of proxies and firewalls, but its HTTP-compatible handshake lets it pass through HTTP infrastructure, though some proxies break it.

facts.text: The handshake is HTTP-compatible, so HTTP servers can share ports 80 and 443 with a WebSocket gateway or server; behind a configured proxy, the client sets up a persistent tunnel with HTTP CONNECT.
Some proxies are transparent and work with WebSocket, others make the connection fail; unencrypted traffic through a proxy without WebSocket support will likely fail.

Encrypted WebSocket Secure connections succeed more often: with an explicit proxy TLS ensures HTTP CONNECT is issued, and transparent proxies let encrypted traffic through; connections on port 443 are significantly more likely to succeed than on port 80.

A server may offload the connection to load balancers and reverse proxies; the RFC counts everything from the first device that terminates the TCP connection to the server that processes requests as the server.

With load balancers and multiple servers, a dedicated set of hosts for WebSocket connections, separate from the HTTP servers, is probably easier to manage, because interactive messaging traffic can induce unusual loads on some components.

Load balancers must support persistent connections so a server can keep a connection such as a WebSocket open with a client; nginx can act as reverse proxy and load balancer for WebSocket applications.

definition.text: The WebSocket API is the browser interface through which a web application opens a WebSocket, sends messages and reacts to events.

facts.text: The constructor new WebSocket(url [, protocols]) starts the opening handshake; the URL scheme must be ws, wss, http or https, with no fragment, and the default port is 80 for ws and http and 443 for wss and https.
send(data) takes a string, Blob, ArrayBuffer or ArrayBufferView; if the data cannot be sent because the buffer is full, the connection is closed and an error event fires.

The API raises open, message, close and error events; the close event reports a code, a reason and whether the closing handshake completed, with code 1005 when the Close frame has no payload and 1006 when none arrived.
readyState is CONNECTING (0), OPEN (1), CLOSING (2) or CLOSED (3); close(code, reason) accepts code 1000 or 3000 to 4999 and a reason of up to 123 UTF-8 bytes.

title: WebSocket subprotocols
article: rfc>6455#1. Introduction > 1.9. Subprotocols Using the WebSocket Protocol

definition.text: A WebSocket subprotocol is an application-level protocol layered over WebSocket messages, which the client and server agree on in the opening handshake.

facts.text: The client lists the subprotocols it accepts in Sec-WebSocket-Protocol, ordered by preference; the server selects one of those values and echoes it, and must not reply with a value the client did not offer.
Subprotocol names should be registered and should contain the ASCII domain name of the originator to avoid collisions, such as "chat.example.com".
Competing subprotocols with different names can be served at once, with the server choosing dynamically from the value the client sent.

A backward-incompatible change is versioned by renaming the subprotocol, for example to "v2.bookings.example.net", which clients treat as completely separate; a backward-compatible change reuses the same string.

definition.text: WebSocket extensions let implementations opt in to additional protocol features, negotiated during the opening handshake.

facts.text: The base specification defines no extension; the client offers extensions in Sec-WebSocket-Extensions and the server accepts some or all by listing them in its response, never listing one the client did not request.
A client MUST NOT use an advertised extension unless the server indicates it wants to use it; the server's list is what is actually in use for the connection.
Order matters: the client's list is in order of preference, and operations are applied in the server's order, so "foo, bar" makes bar(foo(data)).
Extensions can use the three reserved RSV bits, opcodes 3 to 7 and 11 to 15, and the extension data field; permessage-deflate compresses data messages with DEFLATE and sets RSV1 on the first frame.

title: Reconnect with backoff
article: rfc>6455#7. Closing the Connection > 7.2. Abnormal Closures > 7.2.3. Recovering from Abnormal Closure

definition.text: After an abnormal closure a WebSocket client should wait a random, growing delay before reconnecting, so that many clients do not overwhelm the server.

facts.text: An abnormal closure may be transient, so reconnecting can work, or nontransient, in which case clients that all reconnect immediately and persistently amount to a denial-of-service attack that can keep the service from recovering.
Clients SHOULD use backoff when reconnecting: the first attempt SHOULD be delayed by a random time, and a value chosen randomly between 0 and 5 seconds is a reasonable initial delay.
If the first attempt fails, later attempts SHOULD wait increasingly longer, using a method such as truncated binary exponential backoff.
Terminated WebSocket connections are not automatically recovered.

sources.title: Long polling, WebSockets, Server-Sent Events (SSE) (Singh's System Design)

title: WebSocket version negotiation
article: rfc>6455#4. Opening Handshake > 4.4. Supporting Multiple Versions of WebSocket Protocol

definition.text: WebSocket version negotiation lets a client request a protocol version in the handshake and the server answer with the versions it supports if it cannot accept it.

facts.text: A client states the version it prefers in Sec-WebSocket-Version, which need not be the latest it supports; if the server supports it and the handshake is otherwise valid, the server accepts that version.

If the server does not support the requested version it MUST answer with Sec-WebSocket-Version header fields listing every version it is willing to use, for example with an HTTP error such as 426 Upgrade Required.
If the client supports one of the advertised versions, it can repeat the handshake with that version value.

definition.text: WebSocket defines two URI schemes, ws for unencrypted connections and wss for connections protected by TLS.

facts.text: The port is optional: the default is 80 for ws and 443 for wss, and a URI is called secure when its scheme is wss.
A wss URI indicates that the traffic is protected by TLS, with its usual confidentiality, integrity and endpoint authentication.
The resource name that the handshake requests is the path plus any query, or "/" when the path is empty, which lets one host and port serve several services.
Fragment identifiers are meaningless in WebSocket URIs and MUST NOT be used.

definition.text: Comet is a web application model in which a long-held HTTPS request lets a web server push data to a browser without the browser explicitly requesting it.

facts.text: Comet is an umbrella term for several techniques that give the browser two-way sustained interaction with the server, all relying on default browser features such as JavaScript rather than plugins.

Implementations fall into streaming, which keeps one persistent connection for all events (a hidden iframe filled with script tags, or XMLHttpRequest), and long polling, where each response ends the request and the browser opens a new one.

No streaming transport works in every browser, so many applications use long polling, which works wherever XHR does; a held connection can block other requests under HTTP 1.1's connection advice, so a separate hostname is used (domain sharding).
The standardisation of WebSocket and Server-sent events, widely supported since 2020, has rendered the Comet model obsolete.

definition.text: The C10k problem was the problem of optimizing networking stacks to handle ten thousand concurrent clients at the same time.

facts.text: Handling many concurrent connections differs from handling many requests per second: the latter needs high throughput, the former needs efficient scheduling of connections to sockets or other stateful endpoints.
Supporting many clients involves operating system constraints and web server limits, a choice between multi-threading and single threading, memory management, and the strategy for I/O.
The problem is solved: by the early 2010s a commodity server held millions of connections, for example WhatsApp over 2 million with Erlang and MigratoryData 10-12 million with Java.

Nginx was originally developed to solve C10k and handles more than 10,000 simultaneous connections with a low memory footprint; very high connection counts matter for proxy servers, web servers and load balancers.

definition.text: XMPP is an open, XML-based communication protocol for instant messaging, presence information and contact list maintenance, enabling near-real-time exchange of structured data between network entities.

facts.text: XMPP is extensible well beyond chat, serving as message-oriented middleware for VoIP signalling, video, file transfer and gaming, and it is defined in an open standard at the application layer.
The network is federated like email: anyone can run a server, there is no central master server, and users on any server interoperate through a Jabber ID.

A client sends a message to its own server, which delivers it instantly if the recipient is online and otherwise holds it; for a user on another server, the first server connects to that server over XMPP.

Clients reach servers over a TLS-encrypted TCP stream on port 5222 and servers talk to each other on port 5269; the core RFC 6120 uses two open-ended XML streams carrying presence, message and iq stanzas.
A Jabber ID looks like an email address, username@domain; an optional /resource suffix names one of the user's clients, such as home, work or mobile, so one user can log in from several places.
The native transport is long-lived TCP; for web clients and firewalled users there is BOSH over HTTP, which lets the server push messages as soon as they are sent, and XMPP can also use WebSockets.
Extensions called XEPs add features such as multi-user chat, Jingle for peer-to-peer VoIP sessions and OMEMO end-to-end encryption, so the server operator cannot decrypt the data it forwards.
Because XML is text, XMPP has higher network overhead than binary protocols, and in-band binary data must be base64 encoded, so large transfers such as files are best sent out-of-band.

definition.text: Presence information is a status indicator that conveys the ability and willingness of a potential communication partner to communicate.

facts.text: A client publishes a presence state to a presence service, which stores it as the user's personal availability record (the presentity) and distributes it to interested users, called watchers.
Presence is usually shown as an icon with states such as free for chat, busy, away or do not disturb; standards also allow attributes such as mood, location or free text.

Presence from several devices can be aggregated and inferred from observation, such as marking a user Away when the keyboard is idle; XMPP gives each client a resource and a priority, and messages go to the highest.
Presence is highly sensitive, so a presentity may limit what each watcher sees; a basic form is the blocking facility, which makes a user appear unavailable to selected watchers.

definition.text: Web push lets an application server control how long, how urgently and in what form a push message is held and delivered, through the TTL, Urgency and Topic headers.

facts.text: An application server MUST send a TTL header, in seconds, saying how long the push service keeps the message for intermittently connected devices; the service may keep it for less and MUST NOT deliver it once the TTL elapses.
A message with a zero TTL is delivered at once if the user agent is available and otherwise expires undelivered, so the application server cannot rely on acknowledgement receipts for it.

The Urgency header (very-low, low, normal, high; normal by default) helps battery-powered devices stay dormant: a user agent can state the lowest urgency it will accept, and the service MUST NOT deliver anything lower.
A message with a Topic header of up to 32 characters replaces any outstanding message with the same topic, so a device that was offline does not receive outdated or redundant messages.

sources.title: RFC 8030: Generic Event Delivery Using HTTP Push

definition.text: A push service must hold very many open connections and stored messages, deliver reliably, and be secured with TLS, end-to-end encryption and rate limits.

facts.text: A push service holds a very large number of open TCP connections and can redistribute load with 307 redirects or HTTP alternative services; storing messages for their TTL can also take a significant amount of storage.

Reliable delivery with receipts avoids retransmissions, polling and state resynchronization; without it a device must acknowledge directly to the application server at extra power cost, though transient messages such as an incoming call may not need reliability.

The protocol MUST use HTTP over TLS, but TLS does not hide content from the push service, so applications MUST add end-to-end confidentiality, integrity and authentication, as Message Encryption for WebPush does.

Push URIs should be hard to guess and shared only with authorized application servers; a push service SHOULD limit the message rate per user agent, can answer 429 with Retry-After, and may end subscriptions that get too many messages.
